caption:
I didn’t plan this. I just reacted.

She saw the nebulizer mask and her whole body tensed up. Eyes wide. That look that says “I’m about to lose it.”

And everything in me wanted to say “it’s okay, there’s nothing to be scared of, it doesn’t hurt, I promise.”

But I know that doesn’t work. Not because she’s being difficult but because her survival brain was already running the show. And you can’t reason with a nervous system in protection mode.

So I grabbed Dragon.

I held the mask up to her stuffed dragon and said “Dragon, can you show her how it’s done? You’re going to sit so still and be so brave.”

And I watched my daughter’s whole body shift. She leaned in. She reached over and held Dragon’s hand. She was studying what was happening.

When I said “okay, your turn” she did it. No tears. No fight. She even held Dragon against her chest the whole time the mask was on.

Here’s what most parents don’t know: when children watch someone they trust go through something scary first, their nervous system gets a preview. A rehearsal. Their brain registers “Dragon survived. Maybe I will too.”

It’s called borrowed courage. And it works because you’re not asking their logical brain to override their fear, you’re giving their body a signal that it’s safe.

This is exactly the kind of thing I wish every parent knew. Not complicated theories. Just simple, practical tools you can pull out in the moment when things are falling apart.

When your toddler pushes back, refuses, melts down over seemingly nothing, it’s easy to feel like they’re doing it on purpose. Like they’ve figured out the exact buttons to press. 

But here’s what’s happening in their brain…

A toddler’s prefrontal cortex, the part responsible for logic, impulse control, and emotional regulation, won’t fully develop until their mid-twenties. So when stress hits, their survival brain takes over. This means the amygdala fires, cortisol floods their system and suddenly they’re in fight, flight, or freeze mode.

In that moment, they’re not thinking. They’re surviving.

And here’s the part most parents miss: that “testing” behaviour? It’s actually their nervous system doing a safety scan. They’re unconsciously asking, “If I fall apart right now, will you still be here? Will you stay regulated when I can’t?”

This is attachment science in action. Kids need to know their primary caregiver is a secure base. Someone who won’t abandon them, yell, or crumble when things get hard. That’s how they build the internal wiring for self-regulation later.

So when they push, they’re not being difficult. They’re checking if you’re safe enough to be their anchor.

And every single time you stay calm, get low, stay present through the chaos… you’re literally helping their brain build the neural pathways they need to regulate on their own one day.

You’re not just surviving the hard moments. You’re shaping their nervous system 🤍

The whining isn’t manipulation.

I know it feels like it. I know it’s relentless. I know you’ve already answered the same question four times and they’re STILL going.

But here’s what’s actually happening as a pediatric OT:

Their nervous system is stuck in a loop it can’t exit alone.

When toddlers get dysregulated (tired, hungry, overstimulated, or just done) their brain gets caught in this repetitive cycle. The whining, the repeating, the “but whyyyy” on loop? That’s not them trying to break you down.

That’s them signaling: “I’m stuck and I don’t know how to get out.”

They’re not doing it TO you. They’re doing it because they need you. Your calm is their exit ramp.

Not logic, not explaining, not “I already told you.”

Think connection first & then the loop can release.

What does that look like? Get low. Eye level. A hand on their back. Sometimes just sitting next to them without saying anything. Let your body tell their body: “I’m here. We’re okay.”

You don’t have to fix it. You just have to be the steady thing in the chaos.

So next time the whining hits and you feel yourself tensing up, pause. Breathe. Drop down to their level. Their nervous system is looking for yours to lead the way.

caption:
It’s overwhelming, it’s too much & where do you even start?

As a pediatric OT, this is quite common. Parents load the plate with variety hoping something will land. But to a toddler’s nervous system, more options doesn’t feel exciting. It feels like pressure.

And when their system is overwhelmed, it shuts down. They push the plate away. They ask for the one “safe” food again and as parents, we start to worry.

Here’s what actually works:

1. Smaller plate, fewer choices. Three to four foods max. Their brain can actually process what’s in front of them without going into overload.

2. Include one safe food )a food they already love) every time. That familiar food tells their nervous system “you’re okay here.” It’s not giving in. It’s giving them an anchor.

3. Let them watch you eat first. Toddlers learn through observation. When they see you calmly eating the same food, their brain registers it as safe. Try not to add any pressure or performance, just eat your meal. 

4. Food play before food pressure. Let them poke it, smell it, squish it. Sensory exposure builds tolerance. Eating comes later. This is the OT way to support picky eaters. 

5. Stay calm when they refuse. Your nervous system is contagious. If you tense up, they feel it. A relaxed mealtime does more than any bribe ever will.

Picky eating isn’t a battle to win. It’s a nervous system asking for safety.

You’re not failing. You’re learning their language 🤍

Generally, I am quite firm to try my best to avoid screen time altogether for my little one (especially under 2) to support healthy brain development and I know it would just not be worth the aftermath. 

However, whether sick, jet lagged or you just need a moment… sometimes you need a bit of help from the big black box. Generally, it’s a “no” in my house, but making an exception for a short period of time in these situations is understandable. 

If you do choose screen time, try to opt for shows like:
- Puffin Rock (Netflix) 
- Trash truck (Netflix) 
- Guess how much I love you (Prime Video) 
- If you give a mouse a cookie (Prime Video) 
- Llama Llama (Netflix)
- Octonauts (Netflix)
- Cory Carson (Netflix)

These shows offer: 
🌿 Gentle pacing and low-stimulation storytelling to avoid overwhelming developing brains
🤝 Positive themes like friendship, empathy, curiosity, and problem-solving that support social-emotional growth
🎨 Soft colors and calming environments that encourage relaxation and focused attention
🧠 Thoughtfully designed content to nurture early childhood development without overstimulation

Unlike fast-paced, loud and noisy, highly stimulating shows like Cocomelon, these calmer options help toddlers learn and regulate emotions without overwhelming their growing brains.

On challenging days, gentle, well-chosen screen content can be a helpful tool, just remember to co-view with your child when possible and definitely keep screens out of mealtimes and bedtime routines to promote healthy habits. ✨ 

Again, I am not recommending screen time for little ones 📺 but I do know in specific moments in time it can be helpful if you pick the right ones 🫶

Stop rushing. You’ll get there faster.
I know this sounds wrong, but here’s what I mean:

Transitions don’t fail at the transition. They fail sixty seconds before.

caption:
Dinner battles with picky eaters can feel exhausting. Your child refuses the food. You encourage “just one bite.” They say no. You try again.

And before you know it, dinner has turned into a negotiation.

Here’s something many parents don’t realise: picky eating is often not about taste at all.

As a pediatric occupational therapist, I often see children who are actually struggling with the sensory experience of food.

Some textures can feel very intense in a child’s mouth; mushy foods, mixed textures, foods that feel unpredictable. When that happens, their nervous system may interpret the food as something that feels unsafe or overwhelming.

So when we push them to take a bite before they’re ready, their brain goes into protection mode.

This is something we understand well in the SOS Approach to Feeding, a research-informed method used by feeding therapists around the world. One of the core ideas is that children learn to eat through gradual sensory exploration.

Before a child eats a new food, they often need to:
Look at it
Touch it
Smell it
Play with it
Maybe lick it
All of those steps are actually part of the learning process.

So instead of focusing only on the bite, here are three small shifts that can make mealtimes feel calmer:

1. Change the texture - Sometimes a child will accept a food when it feels different. For example, crispy carrots instead of soft carrots.

2. Let them explore the food first- Touching, smelling, and even squishing the food is often how children build familiarity and safety.

3. Always include a “safe food”- When a child has something on the plate they know they can eat, their nervous system stays calmer and they’re more open to exploring other foods.

Picky eating is incredibly common in childhood, and it doesn’t mean you’re doing anything wrong.

With the right support, patience, and a sensory-informed approach, many children gradually expand the foods they feel comfortable eating.

The brain areas responsible for reasoning and language, mainly the prefrontal cortex, temporarily go offline. Instead, deeper brain structures like the amygdala and limbic system take over, activating fight-flight-freeze.

So your child isn’t ignoring you.
Their brain is prioritizing safety over logic.

In early childhood, the pathways between the thinking brain and emotional brain are still developing. This means toddlers rely heavily on bottom-up regulation — regulation that starts in the body before it reaches the brain.

This is where sensory input becomes powerful.
Rhythmic movement like rocking, swinging, or walking stimulates the vestibular system, which helps regulate alertness and emotional stability.

Deep pressure from hugging, squeezing, pushing, or crashing activates the proprioceptive system, sending calming signals through muscles and joints that help organize the nervous system.

These sensory signals reach the brain before language can.

So when a toddler is overwhelmed, the fastest way to help them regulate isn’t through words.

It’s through movement, pressure, and co-regulation.
Once the body settles, the thinking brain can come back online and that’s when words finally start to work.

Did you know there are actually 32 steps before a child eats a new food?

Most parents think eating looks like this:
food on plate → child eats it.

But for many children; especially picky eaters, the brain has a very different process. And this might completely change how you see progress at the table. 

Because before a child eats a new food, their brain may need to:
• tolerate the food on the table
• look at the food
• interact with it
• touch it
• smell it
• bring it to their lips
• lick it
• take a tiny bite and spit it out 
Only after all of these steps does actual eating happen.
In fact… eating is actually the LAST step.

And here’s the part most parents don’t realise:
Touching the food is already progress.
Even smelling the food is progress.
Even licking the food is progress.

This concept comes from the SOS Approach to Feeding, used by pediatric feeding therapists.
Because eating isn’t just about taste. It’s also about whether the nervous system feels safe.

And when children feel pressured to eat…
their brain often shifts into stress mode instead of curiosity mode, which actually makes new foods harder to try.

But when children are allowed to explore food through these tiny steps, something interesting happens. Curiosity starts to grow.
Confidence grows & eventually…
eating often follows.

So if your child touched the broccoli today…
that might actually be step 15 out of 32.

And that’s real progress! 

Parenting picky eaters isn’t about forcing bites.
It’s about helping children move one sensory step closer to eating.

When we shift from controlling behavior to supporting regulation, everything changes.

If this stopped you scrolling, here’s why 👇
Most “tantrums” aren’t about behaviour. They’re about a nervous system that’s overwhelmed and out of capacity.

When a child is dysregulated: • Their brain can’t access logic • Language goes offline • Self-control is biologically unavailable
So asking them to “calm down” or “use your words” often makes things escalate, not improve.

As a pediatric occupational therapist, the biggest shift I see is this: Regulation first. Behaviour later.

Try this instead:
1️⃣ Co-regulate quietly Get low, soften your voice (whisper), slow your breathing. Your calm is the anchor.

2️⃣ Offer sensory support, without forcing touch • Sit nearby (don’t crowd) • Place a rolled pillow, blanket or towel nearby so they can get deep pressure they control (squeezing or leaning into it) versus if they accept your touch, deep bear hug • Offer slow movement like rocking a chair or swaying beside them

3️⃣ Say less Presence > explanations in the moment

4️⃣ When they start to settle, use indirect connection Talk through a stuffed animal or toy:
“Teddy is wondering if you’re feeling okay.” “Teddy would like to offer a hug, you can say yes or no.”
Let the toy ask. Let the child choose. If they accept the teddy’s hug, then they are ready for yours 🫶

If your child pushes you away, they’re not rejecting you. They’re protecting their nervous system.

What looks like “bad behaviour” is often a body asking for support.

caption:
This sounds wrong… but it works.
When a child is dysregulated, their nervous system is in survival mode.
In that moment:
 • The thinking brain is offline • Language is hard to process • Reasoning feels threatening, not helpful

So when we say: “Use your words.” “Calm down.” “Let me explain.”

We’re asking a body in alarm to do a thinking-brain task.
That’s why it escalates instead of settles.
What works faster?

Movement. Pressure. Rhythm. Sensation.
Because the nervous system doesn’t calm through logic  it calms through the body.

This isn’t about “giving in.” This isn’t permissive parenting. And this doesn’t mean we never teach or talk.

It means: ➡️ Regulate first ➡️ Teach later

Once the body feels safe, the brain can listen again.
This is the foundation of sensory integration and it’s why movement often calms faster than words.

If this made something click for you, save it. And if you’ve ever felt confused about why talking makes things worse… you’re not imagining it.

This is exactly what I teach parents in clinic, and it’s often the missing piece.

This simple movement helps their nervous system integrate — boosting coordination, confidence, and resilience.

So next time they reach for that bar… Let them hang. 🌿

As an OT, I know that during a meltdown, it can be really hard for a child to hear an adult trying to calm them down – sometimes, it feels like more pressure. But one thing that can work wonders is using something else to communicate and redirect their focus. That’s where these stuffed animals come in! 🧸💖

Instead of me directly addressing her during a meltdown, I let the stuffed animals ‘talk’ to each other, creating a safe, non-threatening space for her to process her emotions. This little act of imagination shifts her attention and lowers the intensity of the moment. The stuffed animals’ gentle questions – like “Are you feeling sad?” or “Do you want a hug?” – create a bridge of empathy without feeling overwhelming.

By involving something that feels familiar, comforting, and neutral, we help her calm down in her own time, which allows her to self-regulate. This approach is effective because it takes the pressure off and gives her space to reconnect with her feelings in a way that’s less confronting. In moments like these, it’s not about forcing calm – it’s about inviting it gently. 🌟

✨ Ever wondered how kids might stay a little more regulated —even on overstimulating holidays?

It’s about building regulation in throughout the day using movement, pressure, and play. Why? Because the nervous system listens to sensory input long before it listens to logic.

As a pediatric OT (and mom!), I use simple, science-backed strategies:
 ✔️ Tossing her high in the pool = wakes up her brain (vestibular) ✔️ Pulling a laundry basket = grounds her body (proprioception) ✔️ Spinning, climbing, crashing = keeps her system balanced ✔️ Blanket swinging + burrito wrap = the calm-down combo that actually works

🌟✏️ As a pediatric occupational therapist, I love to support a child’s development in their early years. Understanding pre-writing and early writing milestones can help you encourage your little ones as they grow! Here’s a breakdown of what shapes and skills to expect from ages 1 to 5:

✨ 1 Year Old: 
- Focus on exploration! Your child will enjoy tearing paper and making random marks with their fingers. At this stage, they’re not yet recognising shapes but are developing sensory skills.

🖍️ 2 Years Old: 
- Scribbling becomes the main activity! Expect random scribbles, often large and unstructured. However, you’ll start to see vertical and horizontal strokes. They’ll start experimenting with different writing tools, using a fist grip to hold crayons.

🔵 3 Years Old: 
- Shape recognition begins! Your child can copy circles and make horizontal and vertical lines. They’re starting to understand that drawings represent real objects, showing improved control over their writing tools.

✖️ 4 Years Old: 
- More shapes come into play! Little ones can copy crosses, squares and even attempt triangles. They’ll draw recognisable figures like people using basic shapes and can start writing some letters and numbers more accurately

⭐ 5 Years Old: 
- Complex shapes emerge! Children can draw shapes like stars and diamonds and begin to form letters and numbers with precision. At this age, they can write their name and some simple words, showcasing their fine motor skills through activities like cutting and pasting.

Encouraging drawing, colouring, and crafting can significantly support these skills. However, reminder that this is also about how much exposure they’ve had, just like any other skill. Let’s nurture their creativity and development 🎨💕

Hi, I’m Lorena, a pediatric Occupational Therapist and here are some easy ways to use 3 items in therapy sessions that not only engage the kids but also promote essential developmental skills! Here’s how each activity benefits them:

1. Plank Over the Gym Ball 🤸‍♂️
 - This exercise helps strengthen the core muscles, providing stability and support for everyday movements. 
 - It offers proprioceptive input, enhancing body awareness as they learn where their limbs are in space. As well as, receiving deep pressure in the joints through the weight bearing in the hands. 
 - Plus, balancing as they need to maintain their position on the ball and coordination, laying the groundwork for more complex motor tasks!

2. Kneeling on a Gym Ball 🔵 
 - As children kneel and hold onto the ball, they engage their core and develop balance. 
 - This activity can be graded from using a whole hand for support to just one finger, and eventually no hands at all, fostering confidence as they continue to “level up”
 - It also encourages trunk rotation, as they reach for the rings, which is crucial for core stability, balance, coordination, motor skills, crossing the midline, and spatial awareness in children.

3. Backwards Over the Gym Ball 🔄
 - This unique position enhances their vestibular system, promoting balance and spatial orientation through head inversion.
 - As they match rings to cones, they engage their core, further solidifying muscle strength and control.
 - This exercise is fantastic for developing balance and coordination, critical for all physical activities!

Each of these playful challenges supports our children’s growth in fun and engaging way! Give it a try 💪✨

As a pediatric occupational therapist, I love watching little ones hit their developmental milestones! Between 12 and 18 months, they experience incredible growth in both gross and fine motor skills. Here’s what to look for:

👣 Gross Motor Skills:
- Standing Independently: Your toddler may stand without support for a few seconds!
- Walking: Many begin their first wobbly steps, exploring the world around them.
- Climbing & Cruising: Watch them move around furniture, even up it, gaining confidence in their mobility.
- Kicking & Throwing: They can kick a ball and throw it, even if accuracy isn’t perfect!

🖐️ Fine Motor Skills:
- Grasping & Pincer Grasp: Children start to hold small objects and use their thumb and index finger to pick things up.
- Stacking Blocks: Look for them to stack 2-3 blocks, enhancing their hand-eye coordination.
- Turning Pages: They might turn pages of a book, showing their curiosity.
- Scribbling: Watch as they begin to make those first marks with crayons!

Encouraging these activities through play not only supports motor skill development but also fosters communication and cognitive growth. Let’s celebrate these amazing milestones!

A calm corner is a nurturing space designed to help children manage emotions, self regulate & enhance focus. This dedicated area allows kids to take a break from overwhelming situations & practice self-regulation techniques in a safe environment.

Wonderful Options for a Calm Corner:

- Breathing Ball: This tool is brilliant and kids love it! It encourages mindful breathing. By following the ball’s movement, children can learn to slow their breathing, which helps reduce anxiety and improve concentration.

- Weighted Animal: These soft companions provide comforting pressure, which can soothe anxious feelings. The weight offers sensory input that many children find grounding and calming.

- Fidgets: A variety of fidget toys can keep little hands busy, allowing children to release excess energy and focus better. Fidgeting has been shown to help improve concentration for many kids.

- Tactile Boards: These boards offer different textures for children to explore, promoting sensory integration. Engaging with various tactile surfaces can be both calming and stimulating, depending on the child’s needs.

- Headphones: Noise-canceling or soothing sound headphones can help children escape overwhelming sensory input. Listening to calming music or white noise can aid in relaxation and focus.

- Visual Bubble Timer: This visual tool captivates attention with its flowing colors and mesmerizing bubbles. Watching the bubbles move can be a calming activity, helping to slow down racing thoughts and promote mindfulness.

⚠️ please note my model is too young for some of these items ie. fidget is a choking hazard, so please note most of this is for 3+ years. However, it’s great to start them as early as 1.5 years old, without specific items. 

By incorporating these tools into a calm corner, we empower children to recognise their feelings & utilise resources that help them regain control. This supportive area encourages kids to take a moment for themselves, recharge, & return to their activities in a calm state. How I would have loved one of these as a child! 💫

Gross & Fine Motor Skills you may start to see from 19 to 24 Months🌟

As a pediatric occupational therapist, it’s so exciting to watch the milestones that your little ones achieve between 19 and 24 months! These skills are crucial for their development and independence. Here’s what to look for:

👣 Gross Motor Skills:
- Running: Watch them dash around with newfound confidence!
- Climbing: They love to explore by climbing on furniture or playground equipment.
- Balancing: Many can walk along low beams or curbs, enhancing their balance.
- Up & Down Stairs: They may navigate stairs with assistance or independently, improving coordination.
- Hanging: Children start to experiment with hanging from low bars, building upper body strength.
- Turning & Twisting: Increased agility allows them to twist and turn while playing.

🖐️ Fine Motor Skills:
- Inserting Shapes: They enjoy fitting shapes into shape sorters, enhancing problem-solving skills.
- Scribbling: Watch them make those first marks with crayons, expressing creativity!
- Self-Feeding: Using a spoon or fork, they begin to feed themselves, promoting independence.
- Building Towers: Stacking 4-6 blocks helps refine hand-eye coordination. 
- Pointing to Body Parts: They can identify and point to body parts, enhancing language development.
- Simple Puzzles: Completing 2-3 piece puzzles fosters cognitive skills and patience.
- Drinking from a Glass: Transitioning to a glass cup encourages self-sufficiency.

Encouraging these activities through play not only supports skill development but also fosters confidence and curiosity! Enjoy & celebrate these incredible milestones as they grow up way too quickly 🥹

Let me break down how a such a simple & activity can be a powerhouse of gross motor and sensory integration for kids, from a pediatric OT perspective:

💪 Core Strength Superstar: The plank position on the unstable gym ball is a core-strengthening MACHINE! It fires up the deep core muscles (transversus abdominis), those “six-pack” muscles (rectus abdominis), obliques, and lower back. Reaching for those Squigz while balancing adds an extra layer of core challenge!

🏋️ Weight-Bearing Wonder: This activity strengthens little arms, shoulders, and wrists! Weight-bearing provides crucial proprioceptive input (body awareness) to the joints, improving motor control and setting the stage for fine motor tasks like handwriting.

⚖️ Balance: Rolling on the gym ball challenges dynamic balance, forcing kids to constantly adjust their weight and body position. It also stimulates the vestibular system (inner ear), which is essential for balance reactions and coordination.

🧠 Crossing Midline Magic: Strategically placed Squigz encourage reaching across the body’s midline, integrating the left and right brain hemispheres! This is HUGE for bilateral coordination, visual tracking, and even cognitive skills.

🖐️ Proprioceptive Powerhouse: Joint compression during weight-bearing and muscle activation provides amazing proprioceptive feedback, helping kids understand where their bodies are in space.

🐙 Tactile Temptation: Squigz offer a fun tactile experience! Grasping and pulling also provides tactile and proprioceptive feedback to the hands, which is crucial for fine motor development.

👀 Visual Motor Victory: Kids visually track the Squigz and coordinate their movements to reach and grab them, sharpening hand-eye coordination and visual tracking skills!

As a pediatric OT who’s seen the impact of brain injuries firsthand (working in a brain injury unit), I can’t stress enough how important helmet safety is! 🤕 It’s not just about wearing a helmet, but wearing it correctly. Here’s a quick checklist to make sure your little one is protected:

*  Snug Size: Shake test! Should stay put, not slide.
*  Level Position: Covers forehead (1-2 finger widths above eyebrows).
*  Y-Straps: Form a “Y” around ears.
*  Snug Chin Strap: Only 1-2 fingers fit underneath.

Did you know something as simple as climbing *up* the slide can be a powerful boost for your toddler’s brain development? 🧠 It’s more than just playful rebellion; it’s a mini-workout for their cognitive and physical skills!

Here’s the science:

*  Gross Motor Skills & Coordination: Climbing requires toddlers to use large muscle groups in their legs, arms, and core. This strengthens these muscles and improves overall coordination. Each upward movement is a practice in balance and controlled motion.

*  Problem-Solving & Spatial Reasoning: Figuring out how to navigate the incline of the slide involves problem-solving. They have to assess the angle, decide where to place their hands and feet, and adjust their movements as they go. This builds spatial reasoning skills – understanding their body’s position in relation to the environment.

*  Proprioception & Body Awareness: Proprioception is the sense of your body’s position and movement in space. Climbing up the slide provides rich proprioceptive feedback. They feel their muscles working, their weight shifting, and their body adjusting to maintain balance. This enhances body awareness, which is crucial for motor control and coordination.

*  Risk Assessment & Decision-Making: Climbing up the slide presents a small, manageable risk. Toddlers learn to assess the situation, decide if they’re capable of making the climb, and proceed accordingly. This is a valuable opportunity to develop risk assessment and decision-making skills in a safe environment.

*  Cognitive Development: All of these physical and sensory experiences contribute to cognitive development. The brain is constantly learning and adapting as toddlers explore their environment through movement.

So, the next time you see your little one attempting this feat, resist the urge to immediately redirect them. Instead, offer encouragement and support as they conquer this developmental milestone.

Mission Impossible Game🕵️‍♀️ 

As a pediatric occupational therapist, I love incorporating playful activities like the “Mission Impossible” into therapy sessions. This engaging game—where kids maneuver several rings across a stick (“laser”) without touching it—offers incredible benefits across multiple developmental areas:

1. Core Strength: Balancing in various positions while moving the ring requires a stable core. Children activate their abdominal muscles, which is crucial for overall stability and posture.

2. Bilateral Integration: This game encourages the use of both hands in a coordinated manner. By manipulating the ring with one hand while stabilising their body with the other, children enhance their ability to integrate movements across both sides of the body.

3. Proprioceptive Input: Navigating this task provides rich proprioceptive feedback, helping children develop awareness of their body position in space. This is essential for coordination and motor planning. It also provides plenty of “heavy work” as they are stabilising their body weight. 

4. Crossing Midline: As children reach across their body to move the ring, they practice crossing the midline, an important skill for tasks such as reading and writing.

5. Hand-Eye Coordination: This game sharpens visual-motor skills as kids must track the ring and adjust their movements accordingly, improving their hand-eye coordination.

Grading the Activity: 
- Start on all fours to build foundational strength and stability.
- Progress to a plank position for increased challenge and core engagement.
- Finally, balance on a gym ball to further enhance stability and proprioceptive input, making it a fun challenge!

Incorporating this game into therapy not only makes skill-building enjoyable but also reinforces essential developmental skills in a playful context. Let’s keep moving and learning! 🎉💪✨

caption:
Car Seat Safety for Our Little Ones! 🚗💕

As a pediatric OT, I want to remind parents about the importance of limiting time in car seats for babies under 1. The maximum recommended time a child should be in a car seat is about 1 to 2 hours at a time. It’s important not to keep a baby in a car seat for extended periods for several reasons related to their physical development and safety. For example:

1. Posture and spinal development: Babies have underdeveloped neck and back muscles. Prolonged sitting in a car seat can lead to poor posture, which may affect spinal alignment and development.

2. Airway compromise: If a baby is in a car seat for too long, especially if they are angled incorrectly, their airway can become compromised. This can lead to breathing difficulties or a condition known as positional asphyxia.

3. Overall development: Babies need opportunities for social interaction, tummy time, and movement to support their overall development. Staying in a car seat limits these important activities.

Of course car seats are essential for safety during travel, however it’s important to limit the time babies spend in them outside of travel to promote healthy development.

If you’re taking longer trips, allow your baby to stretch, move around, and avoid potential risks by taking regular stops to ensure their comfort and safety.🌟

Ready to Start Baby-Led Weaning? Here Are the Key Signs! 👶🥑🍌

As a pediatric occupational therapist and feeding specialist, there are the essential signs that indicate your little one is ready for baby-led weaning (BLW)! 🍽️✨

1. Sitting Up Independently: Your baby can sit well without support. This is crucial for safe eating and helps them manage food better.

2. Curiosity About Food: Notice them watching you eat? If they’re reaching for your plate or showing interest in what you’re having, it’s a great sign they’re ready to explore solid foods!

3. Tongue Thrust Reflex: This reflex, which pushes food out of their mouth, should be fading. If your baby can keep food in their mouth and swallow, they’re likely ready to try new textures.

4. Grasping Skills: Can they pick up and hold objects? If your baby is mastering the pincer grasp, they’ll be better equipped to handle finger foods and bringing food to their mouth. 

5. Age Matters: Most babies are ready around 6 months, but every child is unique! Trust your instincts and observe your baby’s cues. 

⚠️ Always consult with your pediatrician to ensure your little one is ready! 

Remember that it’s normal to be nervous as parents and this is all about exploration and having fun. How exciting they get to try food for the first time! Enjoy the mess 😋🥦🍌🥕

As a pediatric OT and feeding specialist, the general guidelines for how long children should spend in high chairs are based on their age. The general recommendations are:

1. Infants (6-12 months): Infants can spend about 15-20 minutes in the high chair for meals. This time allows them to explore foods and practice self-feeding without becoming overwhelmed.

2. Toddlers (1-3 years): For toddlers, the recommended time in the high chair is approximately 20-30 minutes. This allows enough time for them to eat, explore new textures, and engage in mealtime routines.

3. Preschoolers (3-5 years): Preschoolers can stay in the high chair for around 30-45 minutes. This timeframe acknowledges their longer attention spans and encourages them to participate more fully in family meals or structured mealtimes.

Of course these times can vary based on the child’s individual needs, temperament, and feeding skills. It’s essential to monitor the child for signs of readiness to leave the high chair and ensure that mealtime remains a positive experience.

Signs of readiness to leave the high chair and ensure that mealtime remains a positive experience include:
- expressing discomfort 
- trying to get out of the chair 
- loss of interest and easily distracted 
- appears to be full and satisfied 
- seems cranky or fussy

🌟👣 The Importance of Barefoot Exploration from Birth!👣🌟

As a pediatric occupational therapist, I want to share why it’s vital for your baby’s feet to be free from the start—even without socks! Here’s why:

1️⃣ Nerve Endings & Sensory Input: Babies have a high concentration of nerve endings in their feet. Early exposure to different textures—like soft blankets or cool surfaces—provides essential sensory input, enhancing their understanding of the world.

2️⃣ Grip Strength & Foot Development: Allowing babies to move their feet freely engages tiny muscles that control grip strength. Kicking and wiggling strengthen their arches, promoting healthy foot development and better mobility.

3️⃣ Proprioception: Proprioception—awareness of body position—is crucial. Exploring without shoes gives babies important feedback about their foot placement, helping refine motor skills as they crawl and walk.

4️⃣ Primitive Reflex Integration: Babies are born with reflexes that need integration for movement development. Experiencing different surfaces with bare feet helps facilitate this, and gentle tickling enhances body awareness.

5️⃣ Balance & Coordination: As babies push up and stand, bare feet help develop balance and coordination. Feeling the ground encourages posture adjustments, setting the stage for walking and running.

6️⃣ Confidence & Independence: Freeing their feet fosters independence. When babies can kick and wiggle, they build confidence, encouraging a lifelong love for movement and play.

🦶💖 Let your little ones enjoy the freedom of their bare feet from day one! Embrace tickles, soft surfaces, and sensory exploration—it’s about nurturing their growth every step of the way.

This dual-tasking boosts their brain’s ability to manage balance under pressure—perfect for real-life situations! 

Encouraging friendly competition with siblings or friends adds an extra layer of motivation. So grab some bean bags, and go for it! 💪✨
